title: Does Oregon Have Sales Tax? Sales Tax and CAT Guide
summary: Oregon has no state or local sales tax, but businesses may owe the Corporate Activity Tax (CAT). Learn CAT rules, transaction taxes, and resale certificates.
body_markdown:
## Oregon sales tax at a glance


**State taxing authority** Oregon Department of Revenue


**Oregon sales tax rate** 0%


**Local sales tax rates** 0%


**Combined sales tax rate range** N/A


**Economic nexus threshold** N/A


**Website**[oregon.gov/dor](https://www.oregon.gov/dor)


**Tax line** 503-378-4988


## Does Oregon have sales tax?


Unlike most other states, Oregon[does not levy general sales and use taxes](https://www.oregon.gov/dor/programs/businesses/Pages/Sales-Tax.aspx) on purchases. This means there’s no statewide sales tax and no local general sales tax, though a few cities, such as[Ashland](https://ashlandoregon.gov/YourTaxesAtWork) , tax prepared food and beverages.


Businesses selling to customers in Oregon do not need to calculate, collect, file, or remit sales taxes to the Oregon government. This simplifies financial tracking and compliance for both in-person retailers and ecommerce sellers based in Oregon.


Because Oregon has no sales tax, it has no sales tax nexus threshold, and SaaS and digital products aren’t subject to sales tax. Numeral’s[Oregon Economic Nexus guide](https://www.numeral.com/nexus/oregon) and its guide to[SaaS in Oregon](https://www.numeral.com/blog/saas-sales-tax-oregon) provide more details.


## Oregon Corporate Activity Tax (CAT)


While Oregon does not levy state sales tax, businesses still need to know about other state taxes. The most notable of these is Oregon’s[Corporate Activity Tax](https://www.oregon.gov/dor/programs/businesses/pages/corporate-activity-tax.aspx) , or CAT.


The Oregon CAT is not a form of sales tax or corporate income tax. Instead, it’s a separate tax imposed for the privilege of doing business in Oregon.


This tax applies to a business’s taxable Oregon commercial activity over $1 million. Businesses with $1 million or less in taxable Oregon commercial activity are not required to pay this tax, though they may still need to register or file a return.


“Commercial activity” is defined as the total amount a business realizes from transactions and activity in the normal course of business in Oregon, subject to certain exclusions. Taxable Oregon commercial activity is the amount remaining after the allowed subtraction. The tax is $250 plus 0.57% of taxable Oregon commercial activity over $1 million.


Some items are exempt from Oregon CAT, such as groceries and motor vehicle fuel. Businesses may also subtract 35% of the greater of qualifying cost inputs (generally cost of goods sold) or labor costs attributable to Oregon, subject to limitations.


### How to file and pay Oregon Corporate Activity Tax


Oregon CAT is levied annually, and the return is due on the[15th day of the fourth month after the tax year ends](https://www.oregon.gov/dor/forms/FormsPubs/form-or-cat-instr_106-003-1_2025.pdf) . For calendar-year filers, this is April 15.


If the deadline falls on a weekend or holiday, the return is due the next business day.


Oregon businesses need to know several CAT thresholds:


- **$750,000 in annual commercial activity:** Register for CAT with the Oregon Department of Revenue within 30 days of reaching this threshold. Failing to register on time can result in financial penalties.
- **$1 million or more in annual Oregon commercial activity:** File an annual return. Payment is required only if taxable Oregon commercial activity exceeds $1 million after the allowed subtraction.


Businesses can register through Oregon’s[Revenue Online](https://revenueonline.dor.oregon.gov/tap/_/) portal. However, returns must be filed by mail or through an approved e-file vendor, and cannot be filed through Revenue Online.


Businesses expecting $5,000 or more in annual CAT liability must also make quarterly estimated payments. For calendar-year filers, these are generally due April 30, July 31, Oct. 31, and Jan. 31 of the following year. If a deadline falls on a weekend or holiday, payment is due the next business day.


Failing to file and pay on time can result in[penalties and interest](https://www.oregon.gov/dor/forms/FormsPubs/form-or-cat-instr_106-003-1_2025.pdf) . These can include a 5% late-payment penalty or a 5% quarterly underpayment penalty.


A 20% late-filing penalty applies if tax wasn’t paid in full by the original payment deadline and the return is filed more than three months after the original or extended filing deadline.


Oregon’s interest rates for unpaid taxes can change annually and are[8% for 2026](https://secure.sos.state.or.us/oard/viewSingleRule.action?ruleVrsnRsn=330785) .


## Transaction taxes in Oregon


Although Oregon does not have a state sales tax, it has a few state transaction taxes for specific items and services. These include:


- [Vehicle Privilege Tax and Vehicle Use Tax](https://www.oregon.gov/dor/programs/businesses/pages/vehicle-privilege-and-use-taxes.aspx) **:** 0.5% of the retail price of any taxable vehicle
- [Transient Lodging Tax](https://www.oregon.gov/dor/programs/businesses/pages/lodging.aspx) **:** 1.5% of the cost of transient lodging stays, increasing to 2.75% in 2027
- [Bicycle Excise Tax](https://www.oregon.gov/dor/programs/businesses/pages/bicycle-excise-tax.aspx) **:** Flat $15 tax on the retail sale of new bicycles priced at $200 or more


## Resale and exemption certificates in Oregon


Although Oregon does not have state sales tax, the state’s Department of Revenue still has an official[resale certificate](https://www.numeral.com/blog/resale-certificates) called the[Oregon Business Registry Resale Certificate](https://www.oregon.gov/dor/forms/FormsPubs/or-business-registry-resale-cert_800-002.pdf) .


Retailers can use this certificate when buying goods from an out-of-state seller specifically to resell them. This certificate can exempt the Oregon retailer from paying sales tax in the state where they’re purchasing the item.


To use this certificate, Oregon retailers should fill out the form and submit a copy directly to the out-of-state retailer when making a purchase. Businesses must also be registered with the Oregon Secretary of State before using this certificate.


Out-of-state sellers are not legally required to accept this certificate. Some state governments may also require you to[use their resale certificate instead](https://www.numeral.com/blog/states-that-dont-accept-out-of-state-resale-certificates) .


Oregon doesn’t issue a sales tax exemption certificate.


## Marketplace sales taxes in Oregon


In general, Oregon-based retailers must collect and remit sales tax on taxable direct sales into other states once they cross that state’s[economic nexus threshold](https://www.numeral.com/blog/economic-nexus) , even though Oregon does not have its own sales tax.


[Numeral’s nexus monitoring](https://www.numeral.com/product/nexus-tracking) alerts you as you approach each state’s threshold.


A physical presence, such as employees or inventory stored in another state, can create obligations even below that threshold.


However, if an Oregon-based retailer sells products to out-of-state customers via an online marketplace like[Amazon](https://www.numeral.com/blog/amazon-fba-sales-tax) or Etsy, the[marketplace facilitator](https://www.numeral.com/blog/marketplace-facilitator) generally collects and remits sales tax on those sales.


Marketplace collection does not necessarily eliminate the retailer’s registration or filing obligations. Laws vary by state, so Oregon retailers should review the requirements for each state where they have physical or economic nexus.


## Shipping and delivery charges


Shipping and delivery charges in Oregon are not taxable because Oregon has no state or local sales tax. However, Oregon businesses may need to collect sales tax on shipping and delivery charges in other states.


This depends on whether the business has physical or economic nexus in those states and how those states treat[sales tax on shipping and delivery](https://www.numeral.com/blog/sales-tax-on-shipping) .


## Oregon sales tax recordkeeping and audits


Even though Oregon does not have a state sales tax, the state’s Department of Revenue can still audit other business taxes, such as the Corporate Activity Tax or income tax.


Oregon businesses with sales tax nexus in other states could also be[audited](https://www.numeral.com/blog/sales-tax-audit) by those states.


Because of this, Oregon businesses should keep detailed financial records for approximately seven years. Businesses should keep track of all commercial activity, including sales volume, revenue, profit, and expenses. Businesses should also keep copies of all tax returns and business registrations.


If you disagree with the results of an Oregon audit, you can[file a written appeal](https://www.oregon.gov/dor/Pages/Appeals.aspx) with the Department of Revenue, then appeal to the Oregon Tax Court’s Magistrate Division.

## Oregon sales tax FAQs


**Does Oregon have a state sales tax?**
No. Oregon doesn’t charge a state sales tax, and no Oregon city or county has a general sales tax, though a few cities, such as[Ashland](https://ashlandoregon.gov/YourTaxesAtWork) , tax prepared food and beverages.


**Why doesn’t Oregon have state sales taxes?**
While sales tax ballot measures have been proposed in Oregon, the state’s voters have[rejected them multiple times](https://opb.org/news/article/oregon-sales-tax-failure-history-business-gross-receipts) . As a result, Oregon has no state sales tax.


**Does Oregon have any alternative business taxes?**
Yes. While Oregon doesn’t have a state sales tax, businesses with more than $1 million in annual taxable Oregon commercial activity must pay the Corporate Activity Tax. Registration or filing may be required even if no CAT is owed. Oregon also has transaction taxes on specific items, such as new vehicles and lodging.
